# Source Selection and Availability Bias

**Dimension:** Biases in which sources get selected and which are systematically
excluded — paywall barriers, authority bias toward highly-cited work,
survivorship bias from link rot, zombie citations of retracted work, and
publication bias toward significant results.

All citations reference [citations.md](../citations.md).

---

## Paywall and Access Barriers

Paywalled content creates systematic inequality in what researchers — and by
extension, the LLMs trained on their work — can access [19].

| Metric | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Global South paywalled citation rate | 61% | [19] |
| Global North paywalled citation rate | 66% | [19] |
| Effect size (paywalled access gap) | d=0.64 | [19] |
| Restricted data access (South vs North) | 23% vs 29% (d=1.02) | [19] |
| Audit sample size | N=18,000 | [19] |
| Nigerian researchers: lower reply rate | 31.6% less likely | [19] |
| Pakistani researchers: lower reply rate | 37.4% less likely | [19] |

The audit of 18,000 data-sharing requests found that Nigerian researchers were
31.6% less likely to receive a reply, and Pakistani researchers 37.4% less
likely [19]. This racial and institutional bias in data access means that
research from and about the Global South is systematically harder to obtain,
creating downstream gaps in any system that relies on accessible sources.

## Link Rot and Survivorship Bias

Web-based citations decay over time, creating survivorship bias where older
sources progressively disappear from the accessible record [43][44].

| Time Period | Accessibility Rate | Source |
|-------------|-------------------|--------|
| 0–5 years | 87% | [43] |
| 10+ years | 38% | [43] |
| Supreme Court opinion links (dead) | 49% | [44] |
| Permanent link rot rate (2012) | 5% | [43] |
| Permanent link rot rate (2025) | 15% | [43] |

Link rot has tripled from 5% to 15% between 2012 and 2025 [43]. When 49% of
links in US Supreme Court opinions are dead [44], the problem extends to the
most authoritative documents in the legal system. For agentic research systems
that verify sources by following URLs, link rot means that older but
potentially more foundational work becomes systematically unreachable.

## Zombie Citations (Post-Retraction Citation)

Retracted papers continue to be cited as if valid, and this pattern propagates
into LLM training data [81].

| Metric | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Post-retraction citations NOT acknowledging retraction | 94.6% (directly sourced) | [81] (supersedes [46]) |
| Retracted papers in sample | 7,813 | [81] |
| Citation contexts analyzed | 48,134 | [81] |

**94.6% of post-retraction citations do NOT acknowledge the retraction** in a
primary-sourced study of 7,813 retracted papers, 48,134 citation contexts, and
60 years of longitudinal data (Hsiao & Schneider, *Quantitative Science Studies*
2022) [81]. This supersedes the prior unverified 90%/96% framing from [46]. An LLM
trained on this literature — or an agentic system retrieving these papers —
has no mechanism to distinguish retracted from valid work unless retraction
status is explicitly checked.

## Citation Bias and Popularity Amplification

LLMs amplify existing human citation biases, preferentially generating
references to already highly-cited work [6].

| Metric | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Median citation count gap (generated vs ground truth) | 1,326 higher | [6] |
| Overlap with actual citations | 7% | [6] |
| Models tested | GPT-4, GPT-4o, Claude 3.5 | [6] |
| Papers analyzed | 166 (3,066 references) | [6] |

Generated references have a median citation count 1,326 higher than ground
truth references [6], meaning LLMs systematically prefer famous papers over
the specific works that authors actually cited. Only 7% of LLM-generated
references overlap with the actual citation lists [6]. This creates a
rich-get-richer dynamic where already-prominent work becomes even more visible
while niche, specialized, or emerging work is suppressed.

## Publication Bias

The underlying literature itself is skewed toward statistically significant
results [82].

| Metric | Value | Source |
|--------|-------|--------|
| Significant results: publication likelihood multiplier | 3.9× (55% published favor new therapy vs 14% unpublished) | [82] (direct PubMed source; supersedes [71]) |

Papers with statistically significant results are 3× more likely to be
published [82]. This means the source material available to any research
system — human or AI — over-represents positive findings and under-represents
null results, failed replications, and inconclusive evidence. Separately,
meta-analyses systematically fail to correct for this: only 18% address
publication bias, and just 4% base conclusions on corrected estimates [60].

---

## Gaps and Limitations

- **Paywall bias directionality:** The Global South access data [19] measures
  human researcher access barriers. Whether LLM training corpora have the same
  access distribution is plausible but not directly measured.
- **Link rot and LLM training:** The link rot data [43][44] measures URL
  accessibility. LLMs trained on Common Crawl snapshots may have captured
  content before links died, partially mitigating survivorship bias for
  training data — but not for real-time retrieval in agentic systems.
- **Retraction database coverage:** The primary-sourced 94.6% unacknowledged-retraction rate [81]
  depends on retraction databases being comprehensive. Coverage gaps in
  Retraction Watch and similar databases mean the true rate of zombie citations
  may be higher.
- **Citation count as proxy:** Using median citation count difference [6] as a
  measure of popularity bias assumes citation count correlates with
  "famousness" rather than quality. Highly-cited papers may sometimes be the
  correct references.
- **Publication bias measurement period:** The 3× publication likelihood
  figure [82] is from 1987. Whether the effect has intensified or diminished
  in the open-access and preprint era is not captured by this source.
- **Missing: preprint vs peer-reviewed selection.** No cited study measures
  whether agentic systems preferentially select preprints (accessible but
  unreviewed) or peer-reviewed papers (authoritative but often paywalled).

## 2026-04-18 Update

### Primary-source replacements for previously-unverified claims

| Original claim | Prior citation | Superseded by |
|----------------|----------------|---------------|
| "90% continued citation, 96% fail to mention retraction" | [46] ResearchGate (unverified) | [81] Hsiao & Schneider PMC — 94.6% of post-retraction citations do NOT acknowledge, 7,813 retracted papers, 169,434 citations, 48,134 contexts, 60-year longitudinal |
| "Papers with significant results 3x more likely to be published" | [71] Wikipedia-indirect | [82] Dickersin 1987 PubMed direct — 55% published vs 14% unpublished favored new therapy, p<0.001, ratio ≈ 3.9x |

See [retraction-log.md](../retraction-log.md) for the full supersession ledger.

### New findings

- **Algaba 2025 extension [84]:** 274,951 references generated by GPT-4o across 10,000 papers. LLMs "systematically reinforce the Matthew effect in citations." Generated refs prefer more-recent, shorter-title, fewer-author works. Extends [6] (Algaba 2024, 166 papers) to three-orders-of-magnitude-larger sample with same directional finding.
- **Independent Pew link-rot dataset [85]:** ~1M webpages, Common Crawl 2013-2023. 25% of pages inaccessible. 38% of 2013 pages gone by 2023. News sites: 23% contain broken link. Wikipedia references: 54% dead-link rate.
- **Crawler-blocking ineffectiveness [80]:** BuzzStream analysis of 4M AI citations from 3,600 prompts. ChatGPT-User-blocked sites: 70.6% still cited. GPTBot-blocked: 88.2%. Google-Extended-blocked (Gemini training): 92.3%. ~70% of ChatGPT citations came from sites blocking retrieval bots. Blocking does not neutralize selection; it redirects it (see also [121] for the implication that state-aligned open-access media fills the void).
- **Gender bias in LLM references [122]:** 660 articles across 22 fields. GPT-4o shows persistent male-author preference. Claude shows majority-group bias. Bias amplified in larger candidate pools. Prompt-based mitigation "only modest."
- **Venue-level citation fabrication crisis:** Nearly 300 ACL/NAACL/EMNLP papers in 2024-2025 contain at least one hallucinated citation [83]. 3-13% of deep-research-agent URLs are fabricated with 5-18% non-resolving overall [87]. This is a new sub-category of source-selection failure — not biased selection of real sources but injection of non-existent ones that never entered the selection pool.

### Counter-evidence on retraction detection

- Discovery-agent counter-search identified that proper cross-platform retraction labeling cuts post-retraction citation rates by ~53% (PMC12439187 study) — the 94.6% unacknowledged rate [81] is a measurement of current practice, not of technical impossibility. LibKey's 2025 cross-citation alerting extends retraction detection to papers citing retracted work.

### Open-access trajectory

- The Royal Society transition to 100% OA in April 2026 and the ACM DL's move to full OA in January 2026 materially change the paywall-bias substrate. The paywall concern remains (~40-50% of literature still subscription-only), but the ratio is shifting.
